site.name: Numori
site.tagline: Software that minds its own business
site.description: A family of open-source apps and services built for privacy, with no AI features of any kind. Fairly priced, fully auditable, and yours to leave whenever you like.

banner.label: Work in progress
banner.text: Numori is being built in the open. Nothing is on sale yet and most apps are unfinished.

status.label: Status
status.alphaHint: Usable today, and rough. Expect bugs, missing corners and the occasional breaking change. Your data is safe — exports work — but do not make it the only copy of anything yet.
status.preAlphaHint: Very early. It runs, but pieces are missing and things change without warning. Worth a look if you like watching software get built; not yet worth depending on.
status.developmentHint: Being built. Not ready to install yet — the repository is public so you can follow along, and the description below is our intent rather than a finished product.
status.honestNote: Nothing here is finished. One app is in alpha, one in pre-alpha, and the rest are still being built — every card says which, and none of them says "coming soon" to mean "we have not started".

meta.title: Privacy-first, open-source software without the AI
meta.description: Numori is a family of open-source apps and services — notes, mail, calendar, files and more — built for privacy, free of AI features, and priced as one fair subscription.

hero.eyebrow: Every line of it open source
hero.title: Software that minds its own business
hero.subtitle: Notes, mail, calendar, files, tasks and more. Built properly, priced fairly, and with no interest whatsoever in what you keep inside them.
hero.note: No AI assistants. No tracking. No adverts. Not now, not later.

principles.title: What we actually promise
principles.subtitle: Six commitments. Each one is either visible in the source code or it is not a commitment at all.

private.title: Private by design
private.body: No tracking, no profiling, no advertising, no third-party analytics. Each service collects what it technically needs to function, and stops there.

open.title: Open source, all of it
open.body: Every client and every server, not just the bits that are safe to show. Promises are cheap; a public repository you can compile yourself is not.

noAi.title: No AI, anywhere
noAi.body: No assistants, no summaries, no "smart" suggestions quietly reading your data to justify a valuation. Tools that do the thing you asked, and only that.

priced.title: Priced like a utility
priced.body: One subscription covers the entire ecosystem. The price follows how much storage you need and how many people share it — no per-product tiers, no feature withheld for a higher price, and no "contact sales".

craft.title: Craft over churn
craft.body: Small, careful releases. Keyboard-first, properly accessible, quick on the hardware you already own, and translated by people who speak the language.

portable.title: Yours to take
portable.body: Open formats and one-click export in every app. Self-host the whole stack, or walk out with your data intact. Leaving should be boring.

products.title: One ecosystem, not a bundle of acquisitions
products.subtitle: Everything shares one account, one design system and one set of rules. Here are the pieces we are building first.

donate.title: Most people will never pay us a penny
donate.body: No app needs a subscription and nine of the thirteen need no account at all, so for most of the people using Numori there is nothing to buy. Donations pay for the servers those free apps run on — the storage nodes, the sync relay, the build machinery. No perks, no donor tiers, no name in a credits file unless you ask.

cta.title: Read the code before you trust the pitch
cta.body: Every repository is public, including this website. Have a look at what is finished, what is half-built, and what is still only a plan.

notes.tagline: Notes that do the maths for you
notes.summary: A plain-text notepad with a natural-language calculator built into every line. Write "48 GBP in EUR" or "12% of 340" and the answer appears beside it, no separate calculator needed.

1.title: A calculator that reads English
1.body: Units, currencies, percentages, SI prefixes and variables, all in the same line of prose you were already typing.

2.title: Local first, sync optional
2.body: Notes live on your device and stay there. Turn on end-to-end encrypted sync only if you want them on a second device.

3.title: Exports that are not a hostage negotiation
3.body: Markdown, plain text, DOCX and PDF, all from a menu rather than a support request.

4.title: Genuinely offline
4.body: The desktop and mobile apps bundle everything they need. No network, no degraded mode.

notes.account: Sign in and every note is already there on your next device, end-to-end encrypted. Without an account the app is complete, but each device keeps its own notes.

clips.tagline: A clipboard with a memory and a filter
clips.summary: A clipboard manager that keeps your history on your machine, recognises code and formats it properly, and refuses to record anything from the apps you tell it to ignore.

1.title: Nothing leaves the device by default
1.body: History is stored locally. Sync is opt-in, end-to-end encrypted, and can be turned off without losing what you already have.

2.title: An ignore list that is actually respected
2.body: Name your password manager, your banking app, your terminal. Clips will not record from them, full stop.

3.title: Understands code
3.body: Snippets are detected, syntax-highlighted and pasted back with their formatting intact.

4.title: Locks like a phone
4.body: PIN, password or biometrics, plus a privacy screen so your history is not in the app switcher.

clips.account: Sign in and your clipboard history follows you between machines, encrypted. Without an account each device keeps its own history.

mail.tagline: An email client that is only an email client
mail.summary: A fast, private client for the mailbox you already have — any IMAP or SMTP account, whoever runs it. No assistant offering to write your replies and no engine reading your post. A Numori-hosted mail service will follow later, priced separately from storage.

1.title: Works with the mailbox you already have
1.body: Standard IMAP and SMTP, so it talks to your current provider, your work account or your own server. Nothing to migrate and no address to change.

2.title: Every account, already there on the next device
2.body: Configure your mailboxes once. Sign in to your Numori account on a phone or a new laptop and all of them are set up and waiting, rather than six rounds of server names and port numbers.

3.title: Nothing reads your mail
3.body: No summarising, no smart replies, no categorising by content. The only thing parsing your messages is the client on your own machine.

4.title: Encryption whose keys you hold
4.body: OpenPGP and S/MIME, with keys generated and kept on your device — not escrowed with a provider who could be compelled to hand them over.

mail.account: Sign in once and every mailbox you have configured is already set up on your next device. No adding six accounts by hand on a new phone, and no exporting settings between machines.

drive.tagline: Storage that cannot read what it stores
drive.summary: End-to-end encrypted file storage with ordinary sharing, ordinary folders and no content scanning. Files go up encrypted, and the server never sees the keys.

1.title: Encrypted before it leaves
1.body: Encryption happens on your device. We hold ciphertext and metadata we cannot avoid, and nothing else.

2.title: Sharing without an account requirement
2.body: Password-protected, expiring links that work for people who will never sign up to anything.

3.title: Versions and a real bin
3.body: File history and a recovery window, because "encrypted" should not mean "one mistake from gone".

4.title: Sync that behaves
4.body: Selective sync, sensible conflict handling and no surprise re-uploads of your entire library.

calendar.tagline: A calendar that keeps your schedule to itself
calendar.summary: Encrypted events with proper recurrence, real time-zone handling and invitations that work with everyone else's calendar. Your diary is not training data.

1.title: Encrypted event contents
1.body: Titles, locations, notes and guests are encrypted. What we can see is limited to what scheduling technically requires.

2.title: Recurrence that survives reality
2.body: Exceptions, moved instances and cross-time-zone repeats handled correctly, including the awkward ones.

3.title: Works with the outside world
3.body: CalDAV, ICS subscriptions and standard invitations, so nobody has to join anything to meet you.

4.title: Availability sharing without exposure
4.body: Share that you are busy without sharing what you are doing.

calendar.account: Sign in and your calendars, and the accounts they come from, appear on every device. Without an account each device holds its own.

tasks.summary: Lists, projects, due dates and recurrence, with an offline-first store and keyboard-first navigation. No streaks, no scoring, no nudges.

1.title: Keyboard-first throughout
1.body: Add, schedule, reorder and complete without touching the mouse. Every action has a shortcut.

2.title: Offline by default
2.body: The list is on your device. Sync is a feature you enable, not a dependency you inherit.

3.title: No gamification
3.body: No streaks to break, no productivity score, no notifications engineered to pull you back in.

4.title: Fits the rest of the suite
4.body: Tasks reference notes and calendar entries directly, without a third-party integration in the middle.

tasks.account: Sign in and your lists and projects follow you across devices, encrypted. Without an account the app works in full, on one device at a time.

chat.tagline: Messaging with nothing in the middle
chat.summary: End-to-end encrypted conversations for one-to-one and groups, with metadata kept to the bare minimum and no bots reading the room.

1.title: Encrypted by default, not on request
1.body: Every conversation, including groups, with no downgrade path and no "secret chat" toggle to forget.

2.title: Minimal metadata
2.body: We are designing to hold as little as possible about who talks to whom, and to document exactly what remains.

3.title: No assistants in your conversations
3.body: No suggested replies, no summarising of what you missed, no third party parsing the transcript.

4.title: Self-hostable
4.body: Run the server yourself and federate, or keep a group entirely inside your own infrastructure.

marks.summary: Encrypted bookmarks with full-text search, archived copies of what you saved, and a browser extension that does not phone home about your browsing.

1.title: The extension collects nothing
1.body: It saves what you ask it to save. It does not report the pages you visit, ever.

2.title: Keeps a copy
2.body: Optional readable snapshots, so a dead link is an inconvenience rather than a loss.

3.title: Search that reaches inside
3.body: Full-text search across the pages you saved, not just their titles and tags.

4.title: Imports and exports plainly
4.body: Standard bookmark files in and out. Bring the pile you have accumulated elsewhere.

marks.account: Sign in and your bookmarks and saved page copies are on every device and in the browser extension. Without an account they stay on the one you saved them from.

sheets.summary: A fast, collaborative spreadsheet with a familiar formula language, encrypted documents and no assistant guessing at your intent.

1.title: Formulas you already know
1.body: A compatible formula language, so existing sheets and existing habits both survive the move.

2.title: Collaboration without a middleman
2.body: Real-time editing over the same encrypted sync layer the rest of the suite uses.

3.title: Quick on large sheets
3.body: Built for tens of thousands of rows without the tab becoming unresponsive.

4.title: Open formats both ways
4.body: Native ODS and XLSX import and export, plus CSV for everything else.

sheets.account: Sign in to open the same documents everywhere, and to collaborate. Without an account the spreadsheet is complete, but the files are local to each machine.

forms.tagline: Forms that do not surveil respondents
forms.summary: Build a form, share a link, collect encrypted responses. No trackers embedded in the page, no analytics on the people filling it in.

1.title: Encrypted responses
1.body: Answers are encrypted to you. The service stores submissions it cannot read.

2.title: No tracking in the form itself
2.body: No third-party scripts, no fingerprinting, no IP logging beyond what abuse prevention needs.

3.title: Accessible out of the box
3.body: Keyboard navigable, screen-reader tested, and readable at 200% zoom without you configuring anything.

4.title: Results where you want them
4.body: Export to CSV, or push straight into a Numori Sheets document.

finance.tagline: Budgeting that stays on your device
finance.summary: Track accounts, budgets and spending with everything encrypted and nothing shared. No bank scraping, no data brokers, no offers based on your balance.

1.title: No third-party bank connections
1.body: Import statements yourself. We will not hand your credentials to an aggregator that resells the transaction feed.

2.title: Multi-currency arithmetic that works
2.body: Built on the same calculation engine as Numori Notes, including historical rates.

3.title: Nobody sells you anything
3.body: No sponsored products, no credit-score upsells, no referral commission shaping the advice.

4.title: Reports you can take away
4.body: CSV, ODS and PDF exports, plus a full encrypted backup on request.

finance.account: Sign in and your accounts, budgets and categories are the same on every device. Without an account each device tracks its own.

pdf.tagline: PDF tools that never see your document
pdf.summary: Merge, split, sign, compress and convert entirely in your browser or on your desktop. Files are not uploaded, because the processing happens locally.

1.title: Nothing is uploaded
1.body: Every operation runs on your own machine. There is no server to trust with the contract you are signing.

2.title: The whole toolbox
2.body: Merge, split, rotate, reorder, compress, redact, sign and fill in forms.

3.title: Redaction that actually removes
3.body: Redacted content is deleted from the file, not covered with a black rectangle you can drag away.

4.title: Works offline
4.body: Install it once and it keeps working on a train, on a plane, and on a locked-down network.

auth.summary: The identity service behind every Numori product: sign-in, sessions, devices and recovery. Open source, self-hostable, and deliberately boring.

1.title: One account, every product
1.body: Sign in once. No separate registration per app, and no separate password to lose.

2.title: Strong second factors
2.body: Passkeys, hardware keys and TOTP. Recovery codes you print, not a phone number we can be socially engineered out of.

3.title: Sessions you can see
3.body: Every active device listed, with one-tap revocation and a readable log of sign-ins.

4.title: Standards, not a walled garden
4.body: OAuth 2.1 and OpenID Connect, so you can put your own applications behind it too.

crdt.tagline: The sync layer, and it cannot read a thing
crdt.summary: The conflict-free replication service every Numori app syncs through. It relays encrypted changes between your devices without ever holding a key.

1.title: Zero-knowledge relay
1.body: The server moves encrypted operations around. It has no keys and therefore no view of your content.

2.title: Merges without losing edits
2.body: Conflict-free replicated data types, so two offline devices reconcile cleanly instead of picking a winner.

3.title: Offline is the normal case
3.body: Edit for a week with no connection. Reconnecting is a merge, not a conflict-resolution interview.

4.title: Run your own
4.body: A single container, documented configuration, and clients that will happily point at your server instead of ours.

pulse.tagline: Uptime monitoring, included in your plan
pulse.summary: Watch your own sites and services — HTTP, TCP, ping, TLS certificates and cron heartbeats — with alerts that go where you ask. It also runs the public status page for every Numori service, which is the honest way to show a monitoring tool actually works. Included in the subscription, or self-host it.

1.title: Your monitors, at no extra cost
1.body: Monitoring is normally its own subscription with its own per-check pricing. Here it is part of the one plan that covers everything else, with no separate bill and no upgrade to unlock a shorter interval.

2.title: Alerts without a middleman
2.body: Email, webhooks and RSS, sent from our infrastructure. No third-party status vendor, and no tracking script embedded in a page whose only job is to say a server is up.

3.title: Honest incident history
3.body: Nothing is quietly edited later. Past incidents stay published, with what broke and what we changed — on our status page, and on yours.

4.title: We watch ourselves with it
4.body: Every Numori service is monitored by this, so if it stops working we find out before you do. A monitoring tool nobody depends on is a monitoring tool nobody has tested.

updater.tagline: A ready-made dashboard for over-the-air updates
updater.summary: Ship over-the-air updates to your Capacitor apps without building the delivery service yourself. The usual options are a paid hosted dashboard or a weekend spent writing your own; this is the third one — run it in a container, or get it with the same subscription that covers every other Numori service.

1.title: Self-host it in an afternoon
1.body: A container image and documented configuration. The free tier of a hosted service normally means building your own distribution panel; this is that panel, already built.

2.title: Channels, staged rollouts and rollback
2.body: Production and beta channels, percentage rollouts, and downgrading to a previous build — the parts you would otherwise write yourself and then have to maintain.

3.title: Signed and verifiable
3.body: Every bundle is signed, so a device can confirm an update came from you before installing it. Reproducible builds mean you can confirm it matches the public source.

4.title: Update checks are not telemetry
4.body: The check asks for a version number. It does not carry a device profile or a persistent identifier, so shipping updates does not mean building a tracking database of your users.

ui.tagline: The design system behind all of it
ui.summary: The Tailwind 4 and Vue 3 component library every Numori interface is built from. Accessible, tree-shakeable, and usable in your own projects.

1.title: Accessibility is not a variant
1.body: Keyboard behaviour, focus management and ARIA semantics are part of each component, not a prop you remember to set.

2.title: Take only what you use
2.body: Import a single component and ship a few kilobytes. Nothing drags the whole library along.

3.title: Nuxt module or Vite plugin
3.body: Auto-import in Nuxt, a resolver in plain Vite, or explicit imports anywhere else.

4.title: Documented in the source
4.body: Every component carries its props, events, slots and examples in JSDoc, so your editor already knows the API.

template.tagline: The starting point for a Numori app
template.summary: The project scaffold every Numori application begins from: Nuxt, the design system, i18n, linting, testing and release wiring already agreed upon.

1.title: Decisions already made
1.body: Linting, formatting, hooks, testing and CI configured the way the rest of the ecosystem is configured.

2.title: Every target from day one
2.body: Web, desktop and mobile builds wired up before you write a line of product code.

3.title: Translatable from the first commit
3.body: i18n structure in place, so localisation is never a retrofit.

4.title: Useful outside Numori
4.body: None of it is specific to us. Clone it for your own privacy-respecting application.

meta.title: Pricing
meta.description: Pay for storage and for how many people share it — never for features. Every Numori account gets every app, the same support, and no platform locked behind a higher price. Most of the apps need no subscription at all.

pricing.title: Pay for space and seats. Never for features.
pricing.subtitle: Move the slider. Two things change the price: how much storage you need, and how many of you share it. Every app, every feature and the same support are in every plan, whether you pay two pounds or twenty.

draftNotice.title: These numbers are not final
draftNotice.body: Most of the ecosystem is still being built, so treat this page as our intent. We will publish final pricing before anyone is asked to pay, and we will not raise it on people who signed up earlier.

pricing.everythingIncluded: Storage and seats change the price. Features never do.

planner.storageLabel: How much storage do you need?
planner.storageHint: One pool, shared by every app. Change it whenever you like, up or down.
planner.peopleHint: Separate accounts, private from one another, sharing one quota and one bill. How many you can add depends on how much storage you have — about 25 GB each, because splitting a small quota twenty ways just recreates the free tier.
planner.ctaNote: Nothing to pay yet — the paid services are not live.

1.label: No account at all
1.body: Install and use it. Notes, tasks, calendars, bookmarks, spreadsheets, budgets, PDF tools and the mail client all work in full, offline, with nothing to sign up for.

2.label: Free account
2.body: Adds sync, and the apps that run on a server: {services}. Your data and settings appear on every device you sign in to, encrypted. Includes 2 GB of shared storage, the documentation and the community forum.

3.label: Paying
3.body: Adds storage, direct email support, and extra seats so other people can share your quota. It adds no apps and no features — every one of those is already in the free tier.

levels.title: Three levels, and only the last one costs anything
levels.subtitle: Most apps work before you have registered for anything. An account adds the parts that need a server to remember them. Paying adds room and our time.

included.1: Every app, on every platform it supports
included.3: Uptime monitoring and an update dashboard, included
included.6: Full export in open formats, whenever you like
included.8: Direct email support, identical at every price
included.9: Every feature we ship from now on
included.10: Extra seats, as many as your storage allows
included.title: Included at every price, including the cheapest
included.subtitle: This list does not change as you move the slider. There is no version of Numori with more features in it, and no support tier above the one you are already on.

noFeatureTiers.title: There is no higher tier to be upsold to
noFeatureTiers.body: Most suites spread features across price points so there is always a next thing to sell you: more domains here, longer version history there, “priority” support if you pay enough. We do not have a next thing. Storage is the only cost that genuinely grows when you use more of it, so storage is the only thing we charge for — and once features are not for sale, the roadmap stops being shaped by what can be withheld.

support.title: Paying buys storage and our time
support.body: Free accounts get the software, the sync and the documentation, but not our inbox. Answering email is the one cost that does not fall as we grow: servers get cheaper per user every year, and a reply never does. Advertising support we cannot staff would mean either ignoring the people who wrote in or quietly going under, so we would rather draw the line and say where it is.
support.paidBody: Direct email support from the people who wrote the code, with no priority tier to be upsold to. The same answer whether you pay the least or the most.
support.freeBody: Thorough documentation, a public issue tracker and a community forum we read. Bug reports are always welcome, from anyone, paying or not.

free.name: Free
free.tagline: Enough for notes, tasks, a calendar and bookmarks that follow you about

features.1: Every app that runs on your device, in full
features.6: No expiry, no card, no nagging

selfHosted.name: Self-hosted
selfHosted.tagline: Your hardware, your quota, our code
selfHosted.priceNote: for as long as you like

features.1: Every feature, with no licence fee
features.2: Storage limited only by your own disks
features.4: AGPL-3.0, so it stays open even if we do not

1.title: Nothing is metered separately
1.body: Mail, Drive, Sheets, form responses and archived bookmarks all draw on the same number. No per-app caps to juggle.

2.title: Move between apps freely
2.body: Attach a 2 GB video to an email or drop it in Drive — it costs the same either way, because it is the same pool.

3.title: Change it whenever
3.body: Slide up or down, prorated, effective immediately. Going down only asks you to get under the new quota first.

shared.title: One quota, not a dozen allowances
shared.body: Your storage is a single pool. A month of heavy photography eats into it; a quiet month gives the room back. You never have to work out which app is full.

noSubscription.title: Every one of the {total} apps works without paying
noSubscription.body: Not a trial, not feature-limited, not five-notes-then-pay. Paying adds room, support and the ability to share your quota with other people. It has never added an app.
noSubscription.noAccountBody: Install and use them. Their data lives on your device, so there is nothing for us to know about you.
noSubscription.accountTitle: {count} need an account, and a free one is enough
noSubscription.accountBody: These run on a server that stays awake while your devices do not, so they need to know whose data is whose. A free account covers that, and they draw on your free quota like everything else.
noSubscription.planAdds: So what does paying add? More storage, direct email support, and extra seats to share your quota with. Multi-seat is the one thing genuinely reserved for paid accounts.
noSubscription.donateCta: Use the free apps and want to help? Donations pay for the servers.

1.a: Because we are not funding a sales team, an advertising budget or a data-science department, and because storage genuinely costs less every year. A small, well-run ecosystem does not need thirty pounds a month from you to survive.

2.q: What is the catch with the free tier?
2.a: Two things, stated plainly: 2 GB is plenty for notes, tasks, a calendar and bookmarks, and nowhere near enough for a mail archive or a photo library; and free accounts get documentation and the forum rather than our inbox. The software itself is not cut down. The apps that need almost no storage are the ones you can use forever without paying.

3.q: Why is there no email support for free accounts?
3.a: Because it is the one cost that does not shrink as we grow. Storage gets cheaper per gigabyte every year; a written reply takes the same twenty minutes it always did. A free tier with unlimited support either gets quietly abandoned or takes the company with it. Bug reports are a different matter — those help us, so the issue tracker is open to everyone.

4.q: Why does storage decide the price rather than features?
4.a: Because storage is the only thing that actually costs us more when you use more of it. Charging for features would mean inventing reasons to withhold them, and then the roadmap starts being shaped by what can be sold rather than what should exist.

5.q: So the free tier really has every app?
5.a: Yes, every one. Nine work with no account at all; five need an account and a free account is enough. What the free tier limits is room — 2 GB — and it gives you documentation and the forum rather than our inbox, and a single seat. No app and no feature is held back.

6.a: No. Numori Mail is a client and it is free — it works with whatever mailbox you already have, and a free account syncs your accounts across devices. A Numori-hosted mailbox is a separate product coming later with its own pricing. That is not a way to charge you twice: running mail is a different shape of cost from storage, driven by deliverability, reputation and abuse handling rather than gigabytes, so folding it into a storage slider would make both prices dishonest.

7.q: What happens if I go over my quota?
7.a: Nothing is deleted. Sending and uploading stop until you free some space or slide the quota up, and everything already stored stays readable and exportable. Holding your data hostage over a billing threshold is not something we are willing to do.

8.q: Can I change how much storage I have?
8.a: Whenever you like, in either direction, prorated to the day. The only condition on going down is that you get under the new quota first.

9.q: What happens if Numori shuts down?
9.a: Everything is AGPL-3.0 and self-hostable, and every app exports to open formats. If we disappear, you can run the whole stack yourself or take your data elsewhere. That is the point of publishing the servers too.

10.q: Will you add AI features later once it gets expensive not to?
10.a: No. It is a founding commitment rather than a current preference, and it is the sort of promise that is easy to check: watch the repositories.

11.q: How many people can share one subscription?
11.a: It scales with storage, at roughly 25 GB each: four people on 100 GB, twenty on 500 GB, forty on 1 TB, up to a ceiling of fifty. The ceiling is not a technical limit — 4 TB would stretch to 163 — but past about fifty people you are an organisation that wants a data processing agreement, single sign-on and a support response time, and those are a different product rather than a bigger number on a slider.

meta.title: Donate
meta.description: Most Numori apps are free and need no subscription. Donations pay for the servers that run the shared services, and there are no perks, tiers or badges attached.

donate.title: Donations pay for the servers
donate.subtitle: None of the {total} apps need a subscription, and {free} do not even need an account. That leaves a lot of people using Numori with no way to chip in. This is that way.
donate.intro: Subscriptions pay the people who write the code. Donations are earmarked for the infrastructure underneath: the storage nodes, the sync relay, the build and release machinery. Separating the two means we can promise that the free apps stay free without quietly hoping they will one day be a funnel.

1.title: Servers and bandwidth
1.body: Storage nodes, the sync relay, the database, monitoring and offsite backups. This is the largest share and the one that grows with the number of free accounts.

2.title: Translation
2.body: Paying human translators instead of running the interface through a machine. It is a stated commitment, and commitments cost money.

3.title: Accessibility audits
3.body: Testing with real assistive technology and paying people who use it daily to tell us where we got it wrong.

where.title: Where it actually goes
where.body: In rough order of size. We would rather name three concrete things than say “it helps us keep the lights on”.

how.title: How to donate
how.body: Several options because donation platforms are unevenly available and take unevenly large cuts. GitHub Sponsors and Liberapay pass on the most; PayPal is the one most people already have.
how.note: Monthly is far more useful than one-off, even at a much smaller amount — a server bill is monthly too. But a single donation is genuinely welcome and there is no wrong size.

noPerks.title: You get nothing for it, on purpose
noPerks.body: No badge, no donor tier, no early access, no name in a credits file unless you ask. Partly because rewarding donations turns a gift into a purchase, which changes how it is taxed and complicates something that should be simple. Mostly because the alternative is a second pricing ladder built out of goodwill, and one honest price list is enough.

other.1: Report bugs. The issue tracker is open to everyone, paying or not.
other.2: Translate an app into a language you actually speak.
other.3: Audit the code. It is all public precisely so that someone will.
other.4: Run an accessibility pass with the assistive technology you use.
other.5: Tell one person who is looking for an alternative.
other.title: Ways to help that cost nothing
other.body: Money is the least interesting kind of contribution and often the least useful. All of these help more than a few pounds does.

meta.title: About and manifesto
meta.description: Why Numori exists: an open-source, privacy-first, deliberately AI-free alternative to software that treats its users as inventory.

about.title: Why we are building this
about.subtitle: A short manifesto, and the reasoning we keep coming back to.
about.intro: Most software you rely on is engineered around a business model that needs your attention or your data. Numori is an attempt to build the same tools around a much duller model: you pay a small amount, we run the service well, and nothing else happens.

1.title: Privacy is an architecture, not a policy page
1.body: A privacy policy is a promise about what a company will choose to do. Encryption and local-first storage are statements about what it is able to do. We prefer the second kind and design so that the tempting option is not technically available to us.

2.title: Open source has to include the servers
2.body: Publishing a client while the server stays closed proves very little: the interesting decisions happen where you cannot see them. Every Numori server is public under the AGPL-3.0, which is why we can reasonably ask to be trusted, and why you do not have to.

3.title: Refusing AI is a feature
3.body: We are not against the technology in the abstract. We are against what it currently requires: your private data moved somewhere it can be processed, a running cost that has to be recovered from you, and a category of feature nobody asked for arriving switched on. So there is none of it, anywhere, and there will not be.

4.title: Software should be finished, not fed
4.body: A note-taking app does not need a quarterly redesign. We would rather ship fewer, better-considered releases and spend the difference on correctness, accessibility and speed than manufacture activity to look alive.

5.title: Accessibility is not an extra
5.body: Keyboard navigation, screen-reader support, sensible contrast, reduced-motion handling and real translations are part of the definition of finished. If it only works for someone using a mouse, with perfect vision, in English, it is not finished.

6.title: Fair price, no dark patterns
6.body: One subscription for everything, cancellation that takes one click, no countdown timers, no interstitials asking whether you are sure you want to leave, and no price rise aimed at people already signed up.

7.title: Leaving should be easy
7.body: Every app exports everything, in formats other software can read, without a support ticket. If we have to trap you to keep you, we have already failed at the actual job.

who.title: Who is building it
who.body: A very small team, working carefully rather than quickly. Numori is developed in the open by Erik Bjerke with Yaiza Wadhwani Valderas and TheProcedural Software Ltd, and every repository takes contributions.

cta.title: Check the claims
cta.body: This page makes a lot of assertions. All of them are testable against the source code, including the source of this website.

licence.title: Why the AGPL-3.0
licence.body: The AGPL closes the loophole that lets a hosted service build on open code without giving anything back. Anyone may run, modify and offer Numori as a service; they simply have to publish their changes too. It keeps the ecosystem open even if we are no longer the ones maintaining it.

contribute.title: Contributing
contribute.body: Issues, translations, accessibility audits and pull requests are all welcome. Translation work is especially valuable: we would rather ship a language properly than run machine translation over the interface.
